headline: TikTok to pay $400 million in landmark settlement over US child privacy violations
deck: The penalty, one of the largest in U.S. history for child privacy breaches, resolves allegations that TikTok improperly collected data from users under 13 without parental consent.
body: TikTok will pay $400 million to settle claims that it violated U.S. child privacy laws, the Department of Justice announced Monday. The agreement resolves years of litigation alleging the platform collected and mishandled personal data from children under 13 without obtaining verifiable parental consent. The settlement, one of the largest ever for child privacy violations in the U.S., follows a federal investigation into TikTok’s handling of minors’ information. The company admitted no wrongdoing as part of the deal but agreed to stringent compliance measures moving forward.

The settlement stems from a lawsuit filed under the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), a federal law designed to protect children’s data online. Prosecutors argued that TikTok, formerly known as Musical.ly, failed to adequately safeguard the personal information of young users, including names, email addresses, and other identifiers. The case highlighted concerns about the platform’s rapid growth among younger audiences and its prior failures to implement robust age verification systems. This agreement marks the first time TikTok has faced such sweeping financial penalties in the U.S. for privacy violations.

The Department of Justice confirmed the settlement in a statement, noting that it addresses systemic failures in TikTok’s data practices. The resolution includes a $400 million payment and mandates significant changes to the company’s privacy protocols. Analysts suggest the penalty may signal a new era of stricter enforcement against tech platforms that fail to protect children’s data. The case could also pave the way for similar actions against other social media companies with large youth user bases.

The litigation began after reports emerged that TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly, had collected data from millions of children without proper consent. Federal regulators accused the company of knowingly allowing young users to create accounts and share personal information, despite repeated warnings about COPPA violations. The Federal Trade Commission had previously fined Musical.ly $5.7 million in 2019 for similar violations, but this new settlement escalates the legal and financial stakes for TikTok.

TikTok’s global privacy officer issued a statement calling the settlement an opportunity to strengthen protections for young users. 'We take privacy seriously and are committed to building a safe platform for our entire community,' the statement read. The company also emphasized its investment in new tools to detect and remove underage accounts. Yet critics argue the penalty, while substantial, may not go far enough to deter future violations.

Legal experts say the settlement sets a critical precedent for how regulators handle child privacy cases in the future. The Department of Justice’s involvement signals heightened scrutiny of tech platforms that prioritize engagement over safety. With children increasingly active on social media, the case underscores the urgent need for stronger protections and accountability measures across the industry. The resolution may also encourage lawmakers to push for tougher legislation on digital privacy for minors.

For TikTok, the settlement comes at a pivotal moment as it faces growing regulatory pressure in the U.S. and abroad. The company has spent years expanding its user base globally while battling criticism over its data practices. Earlier this year, TikTok restructured its U.S. operations to comply with demands from lawmakers concerned about national security risks. This settlement adds another layer of scrutiny to the platform’s operations, particularly regarding its handling of young users’ data.
